questions.stem: During a stable MAC case, every monitor is functioning and alarms are set appropriately. The CRNA steps out to grab supplies. Which "monitor" has just been removed that ASA Standard I treats as most important?
options: Continuous waveform capnography with audible alarms
Pulse oximetry with a variable-pitch tone
The ECG with ST-segment analysis enabled
questions.explanation: Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout every anesthetic. No device replaces the provider.

questions.stem: A chart audit of a 3-hour GA case shows continuous SpO2, ETCO2, ECG, and BP every 5 minutes. No temperature was recorded during a laparotomy with large fluid shifts. Which ASA Standard II element is missing?
questions.explanation: Standard II requires continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; a long open abdomen with fluid shifts clearly calls for temperature monitoring.

questions.stem: Under ASA 2.3, how often must arterial blood pressure and heart rate be determined?
options: At least every ten minutes, more often if unstable
Continuously by invasive line in every GA case
At least every fifteen minutes after induction
questions.explanation: BP and HR must be determined and evaluated at least every 5 minutes. The notes add it may be more frequent, never less.

questions.stem: ASA 2.3 requires circulatory function to be evaluated by at least one additional method beyond ECG and BP. Which of these qualify? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The standard lists pulse palpation, heart sound auscultation, arterial tracing, ultrasound peripheral pulse, or pulse plethysmography/oximetry.

questions.stem: The ECG is disconnected for transfer onto the OR table after induction and reconnected 10 minutes later. Under ASA 2.3, when must the ECG be displayed?
options: From induction until leaving the room
When the patient has cardiac disease
questions.explanation: ASA 2.3 requires continuous ECG display from the beginning of anesthesia until preparing to leave the room.

questions.stem: What does ASA 2.1 require during every general anesthetic given with an anesthesia machine?
options: An O2 analyzer in the breathing system with a low-O2 alarm
Arterial blood gases at least once per hour of anesthesia
A pulse oximeter with an alarm set to 90% or lower
A paramagnetic analyzer placed in the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: Inspired oxygen concentration in the breathing system must be measured by an analyzer with a low-concentration alarm.

questions.stem: During GA, the gas analyzer shows FiO2 0.50 and FeO2 0.45. What does this difference reflect?
options: Expected oxygen uptake by the patient
A circuit leak drawing in room air
Hypoxic gas delivery from the machine
questions.explanation: Expired O2 is lower than inspired O2 because the patient consumes oxygen. Monitoring both shows what goes in and what comes out.

questions.stem: During GA with an ETT, a provider relies on chest rise and breath sounds because the capnograph "keeps alarming." What does ASA 2.2 require?
options: Continual expired CO2 monitoring plus clinical signs
Expired CO2 at intubation and extubation
Expired CO2 when SpO2 falls below 92%
questions.explanation: Clinical signs help, but ASA 2.2 requires continual expired CO2 monitoring.

questions.stem: On a Monday morning, the first case shows a rising inspired CO2 baseline. The machine sat over the weekend with high fresh gas flow running. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Desiccated or exhausted absorbent allowing rebreathing
Hypoxic gas delivery from the pipeline
Dilution of the sample by room air
Complete loss of the capnography sampling line
questions.explanation: Desiccated or exhausted CO2 absorbent allows rebreathing, seen as a nonzero inspired CO2 baseline.

questions.stem: Three cases are scheduled: a 15-minute knee scope, a 4-hour open colectomy, and a cardiac case with planned cooling. In which cases is temperature monitoring required under ASA 2.4?
options: The colectomy and the cardiac case
The colectomy only, since cooling is monitored by the perfusionist
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring is required when significant changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected, as with long open cases and planned cooling.

questions.stem: A patient receives rocuronium at induction. No twitch monitor is used, and you extubate based on a 5-second head lift. What does AANA Standard 8e require?
options: NM monitoring when reversal will not be given
NM monitoring for cases over 2 hours
questions.explanation: AANA 8e requires monitoring NM response for depth and recovery, using quantitative monitoring when available.

questions.stem: Before reversing rocuronium at the end of a case, you want the most reliable measure of recovery. Which method should you use?
options: A visual twitch count at the ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: Quantitative monitoring with a TOF ratio is preferred because qualitative methods miss residual block.

questions.stem: A department reviews hypoventilation-related closed claims. What pattern was found across every one of them?
options: Failure to monitor oxygenation with pulse oximetry
questions.explanation: Every hypoventilation claim involved failure to monitor ventilation.

questions.stem: Of 100 anesthesia closed claims reviewed, about how many would you expect to involve errors in judgment?
questions.explanation: More than 65% of closed claims involved errors in judgment.

questions.stem: Which event type is the most common preventable cause of claims and payouts?
questions.explanation: Respiratory events are the most common preventable cause of claims and payouts.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews airway claims before and after universal capnography. Which adverse event would you expect to have dropped the most?
questions.explanation: Capnography significantly reduced unrecognized esophageal intubation.

questions.stem: On a long overnight case, the CRNA has been awake 20 hours, music is loud, and he checks his phone between vitals. Which factors impair his vigilance? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: External distractions, human factors such as fatigue, and self-initiated distractions such as phones all impair vigilance.

questions.stem: After a hypoxic event, a provider blames "a faulty ventilator." The device later checks out normally. What does outcome data say about this pattern?
options: Device failure rarely causes adverse outcomes
Device failure is the leading cause of adverse outcomes
Device failure causes half of adverse outcomes
Device failure causes most hypoxic events
questions.explanation: Adverse outcomes are rarely due to device malfunction; user error and failure to check are far more common.

questions.stem: Misuse of which equipment was about three times more prevalent among closed claims?
questions.explanation: Misuse of gas delivery systems was 3x more prevalent among closed claims.

questions.stem: A new CRNA cannot find the ventilator's PEEP control and skips the machine check because "it was checked yesterday." What are the most frequent causes of equipment mishaps?
questions.explanation: Most equipment-related mishaps come from unfamiliarity and failure to check, not device failure.

questions.stem: The first case of the day starts without a machine check because "the night team used it." Which AANA standard is violated?
options: Standard 9: alarm limits must be used
questions.explanation: AANA Standard 5 requires verifying anesthesia equipment function before each anesthetic.

questions.stem: During a case, the SpO2 alarm limit is set to 70% and the volume is muted. Which AANA standard does this violate?
questions.explanation: Standard 9 requires appropriate alarm limits and audible warnings.

questions.stem: While drawing up drugs, you hear the pulse oximeter tone drop in pitch and look up to find SpO2 at 89%. Which feature allowed this?
options: A fixed tone at every heartbeat
A visual alarm on the screen
questions.explanation: Variable-pitch tones let you hear desaturation without looking at the monitor.

questions.stem: Which factors contribute to alarm fatigue? (Select 2)
options: Difficulty localizing alarms in a noisy room
Turning alarm volumes to a clearly audible level
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue comes from frequent noncritical or false alarms and difficulty localizing alarms in noise. Audible, well-set alarms reduce it.

questions.stem: What are the results of alarm fatigue? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue leads to ignoring or disabling alarms and missed critical events.

questions.stem: A healthy marathon runner has a resting HR of 48, and the low HR alarm (set at 50) sounds constantly. What is the BEST response?
options: Adjust the limit while keeping it within practice standards
Turn the HR alarm off since the rate is baseline
Keep the default limit and adjust the volume
Turn the low HR alarm to 40 for every athlete
questions.explanation: Alarm limits can be individualized, but the new settings must still meet practice standards.

questions.stem: SpO2 reads 86% with a noisy waveform. The provider assumes it is a poor signal and silences the alarm without checking the patient. What error occurred?
options: Cognitive bias leading to a dismissed valid alarm
Appropriate artifact filtering to prevent fatigue
Correct use of variable-pitch tone recognition
Alarm fatigue caused by default settings
questions.explanation: Assuming artifact without checking the patient is cognitive bias. Every alarm must be evaluated.

questions.stem: The ETCO2 low alarm sounds briefly during a stable laparoscopy, then clears. What is the BEST response?
options: Evaluate the cause even though it cleared
Recheck the alarm limits before assessing the patient
Check monitor settings before the patient
Increase fresh gas flow and observe
questions.explanation: Every alarm needs evaluation of its cause, even when it self-resolves.

questions.stem: A new CRNA says, "The monitors will tell me if something is wrong." What is the problem with this view?
options: Monitors must be interpreted and acted on by the provider
Technology alone prevents most patient harm
Monitors reduce the need for clinical assessment
Alarms replace a systematic sweep of the room
questions.explanation: Monitors are tools. Their data must be interpreted and acted upon by the provider.

questions.stem: Every 5 minutes, you scan from the patient's face across the monitors, machine, IV lines, and surgical field. What is this technique?
questions.explanation: A sweep is a methodical scan of patient, equipment, and field.

questions.stem: Which senses does proactive vigilance use? (Select 3)
options: Monitor trends reviewed after the case
questions.explanation: Use sight, hearing, smell, touch, and technology.

questions.stem: During your machine sweep at hour 3 of a case, which items should you check? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The machine sweep includes vaporizer level, water trap, absorbent color, and the capnogram.

questions.stem: Which patient items belong in the sweep? (Select 2)
options: Eyes taped and free from pressure
questions.explanation: The patient sweep covers positioning, eyes, pressure points, secure lines, and functional IVs.

questions.stem: Which surgical field items belong in the sweep? (Select 4)
options: Blood loss in laps, suction, and floor
questions.explanation: The field sweep covers case status, blood loss, drapes, surgeon communication, and fire risk.

questions.stem: You are using MS MAID to set up your room. What should you check first?
questions.explanation: MS MAID: Machine, Suction, Monitors, Airway, IV, Drugs. The machine check comes first.

questions.stem: During your MS MAID machine check, which items belong under "Machine"?
options: Full check plus a bag-mask and spare O2 cylinder
The vaporizer level and ventilator settings
The CO2 absorbent and water trap
questions.explanation: The machine portion includes a full checkout plus a resuscitation bag-mask and a spare O2 cylinder.

questions.stem: At induction, the patient vomits and the suction tubing is connected but the canister valve is closed. What should the MS MAID suction check have confirmed?
options: Suction on, working, and in reach
Suction was connected for RSI cases
questions.explanation: Suction must have canister, tubing, and Yankauer, and be on, working, and in reach.

questions.stem: Which airway items should be available in the room per MS MAID? (Select 4)
options: Extra blade, handle, and ETT sizes
questions.explanation: The room should have an LMA, extra blades/handles, ETT sizes, stylet, lubricant, syringe, OPA, and NPA.

questions.stem: You set up for a "routine" ETT case with a healthy patient. Which rescue device should be in the room for every case?
options: A cricothyrotomy kit opened on the field
questions.explanation: An LMA should always be available as a rescue device when mask ventilation or intubation fails.

questions.stem: During a power outage, the video laryngoscope will not turn on and the backup monitor's battery is dead. Which MS MAID note was missed?
questions.explanation: The MS MAID setup includes making sure spare batteries and battery-powered equipment work.

questions.stem: A patient enters the OR and you begin applying monitors. Which should go on first?
questions.explanation: The sequence starts with SpO2, then preoxygenation by mask, then BP, then ECG with a baseline strip.

questions.stem: During preoxygenation, what end point does the pre-induction slide use?
options: FiO2 100% for 3–5 minutes or expired O2 ≥90%
FiO2 50% for 1 minute or expired O2 ≥60%
questions.explanation: Preoxygenate 3–5 minutes or until expired O2 ≥90%.

questions.stem: You need both hands to draw up drugs during preoxygenation of a patient who cannot hold the mask. What helps keep the seal?
options: A loose mask with higher flow
An oral airway without a mask
questions.explanation: Head straps maintain the mask seal while your hands are free for other tasks.

questions.stem: After placing an LMA, you hear breath sounds bilaterally but have not checked ETCO2. What does ASA require to verify placement?
questions.explanation: ASA requires verification by clinical assessment and identification of expired CO2.

questions.stem: How long must continual ETCO2 analysis be in use for an ETT or SGA?
options: From placement until removal or transfer to postop care
From placement until the end of surgery
During the first 30 minutes after placement
questions.explanation: ETCO2 is monitored from placement until extubation/removal or initiating transfer.

questions.stem: What must be in continuous use when ventilation is controlled by a mechanical ventilator?
options: A device that detects breathing system disconnection with an audible alarm
A second capnograph on the expiratory limb
A backup ventilator and bag immediately available in the room
A processed EEG monitor for depth
questions.explanation: ASA requires a disconnect detection device with an audible alarm during mechanical ventilation.

questions.stem: During MAC with moderate or deep sedation, how is ventilation evaluated?
options: Qualitative signs plus continuous exhaled CO2
SpO2 alone with a low alarm limit
questions.explanation: Moderate/deep sedation requires qualitative signs and continuous exhaled CO2.

questions.stem: During regional anesthesia with minimal or no sedation, how is ventilation evaluated?
options: Continual observation of qualitative clinical signs
Arterial blood gases drawn at the start and every hour
questions.explanation: With minimal or no sedation, qualitative clinical signs are required.

questions.stem: Which multisensory findings help verify airway placement? (Select 2)
options: A normal blood pressure after intubation
Smell of volatile at the patient's nose
questions.explanation: Condensation and chest excursion verify airway placement along with breath sounds and ETCO2. Blood pressure says nothing about tube position.

questions.stem: After intubation, you see one capnogram waveform, then a flatter one. How many full consecutive waveforms should you see before calling placement confirmed?
questions.explanation: This lecture requires three full consecutive ETCO2 waveforms. (Phases of GA used six; know which your instructor tests.)

questions.stem: During a case, you notice a sweet smell near the machine. Why does the multisensory vigilance approach include smell?
questions.explanation: Smell can detect volatile leaks from the vaporizer or circuit.

questions.stem: Two hours into a stable case, all vitals are normal. Which approach to vigilance is correct?
options: Vigilance is needed mainly during induction
Vigilance can be delegated to alarms
Vigilance relaxes once the patient is stable
questions.explanation: Vigilance must remain constant throughout the anesthetic.

questions.stem: A facility's policy allows NIBP every 10 minutes during GA "to reduce cuff trauma." Which source defines the minimum standard of care?
options: The ASA and AANA monitoring standards
Facility policy, which overrides national standards
questions.explanation: ASA and AANA standards define the standard of care, which requires BP at least every 5 minutes.

questions.stem: The notes say "GETA backup to everything." What does this imply for MAC or regional cases?
options: Be ready to convert to general anesthesia with an ETT
Start with GETA before any regional technique
Avoid regional in patients who may need GETA
Keep GETA equipment outside the room until needed
questions.explanation: Every plan needs GETA as backup.

questions.stem: Which drug categories does MS MAID list? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Drugs span preop, blocks, induction, maintenance, emergence, emergency, transport, and PACU.

questions.stem: You are setting up IV equipment for a trauma laparotomy. Which items belong in your IV setup? (Select 3)
options: A fluid warmer and adequate IV size and number
An arterial line for every case
questions.explanation: IV setup includes fluid type, lines, pumps, rapid infuser, warmer, and appropriate access.

questions.stem: What is the standard ASA monitor list on the MS MAID slide?
options: ECG, NIBP, ETCO2, SpO2, EMG, Fi and Fe gases
ECG, arterial line, SpO2, and processed EEG
questions.explanation: Standard ASA monitors listed are ECG, NIBP, ETCO2, SpO2, electromyography, and inspired/expired gases.

questions.stem: Why is it important to know where you are in the case timeline?
options: To anticipate stimulation, blood loss, and emergence
To tell the surgeon how long they have left
To schedule the next case start time
To time breaks for the anesthesia team members
questions.explanation: Knowing case status helps anticipate critical points.

questions.stem: A department installs advanced monitoring and expects adverse events to disappear. What is the BEST response?
options: Monitors help but do not prevent harm without action
Monitors prevent most harm when alarms are set correctly
Monitors replace the need for interpretation
questions.explanation: Technology supports care, but harm is prevented only when providers interpret and act on the data.

questions.stem: During a case, PIP rises from 20 to 35 while plateau pressure stays at 17. Which compliance has changed?
options: Both static and dynamic compliance equally
questions.explanation: PIP reflects dynamic compliance, which includes airway resistance; a stable plateau shows static compliance is unchanged.

questions.stem: A patient's tidal volume is 500 mL, plateau pressure is 25, and PEEP is 5. What is his static compliance?
questions.explanation: Static compliance = Vt ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 mL/cmH2O.

questions.stem: In a patient without lung disease, how do PIP and plateau pressure compare?
options: PIP equals or is slightly greater than plateau
PIP is at least 15 cmH2O above plateau
Plateau is higher than PIP in normal lungs
Plateau exceeds PIP at normal flows
questions.explanation: Normally PIP is equal to or only slightly above plateau pressure.

questions.stem: PIP and plateau pressure both rise by the same amount. What does this imply?
options: Increased tidal volume or decreased compliance
Increased airway resistance or inspiratory flow
A circuit leak with lower delivered volume
questions.explanation: A parallel rise in PIP and plateau means higher Vt or lower pulmonary compliance.

questions.stem: PIP rises while plateau pressure stays the same. What does this signal?
options: Increased airway resistance or inspiratory flow
Increased tidal volume set on the ventilator
questions.explanation: PIP up without plateau change means increased airway resistance or inspiratory gas flow.

questions.stem: Refer to the airway pressure traces. What does Trace J (PIP 38, Pplat 19) MOST suggest?
options: Increased airway resistance, such as a kink or bronchospasm
Decreased lung compliance from abdominal insufflation
A larger tidal volume set on the ventilator
A circuit leak reducing the delivered volume
questions.explanation: The big gap between PIP and plateau points to resistance, not compliance. Kinks, secretions, and bronchospasm fit.

questions.stem: Refer to the airway pressure traces. What does Trace K (PIP 36, Pplat 33) MOST suggest?
options: Decreased compliance, such as insufflation or pneumothorax
Increased resistance from a kinked ETT
Secretions partially occluding the tube lumen during inspiration
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together, so compliance fell or Vt rose. Pneumoperitoneum, pneumothorax, or position change fit.

questions.stem: PIP rises from 22 to 38 while plateau is unchanged. What is the quickest bedside step to rule out secretions or a kinked ETT?
options: Pass a suction catheter down the tube
Increase inspiratory flow and recheck PIP
Order a chest X-ray before any change
Switch from volume to pressure control
questions.explanation: A suction catheter quickly identifies kinks or secretions.

questions.stem: Which causes increase PIP WITHOUT changing plateau pressure? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Resistance problems such as a kinked tube or bronchospasm raise PIP alone. Larger tidal volumes and compliance changes raise both PIP and plateau.

questions.stem: Which causes increase BOTH PIP and plateau pressure? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Compliance changes and larger volumes raise both pressures.

questions.stem: A student draws a pressure-volume loop with pressure on the vertical axis. What is the correct orientation?
questions.explanation: The P-V loop plots volume on the vertical axis against airway pressure on the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: After a patient is placed in steep Trendelenburg, the P-V loop flattens and rotates toward the pressure axis. What does this loop primarily assess?
questions.explanation: P-V loops primarily assess compliance; flattening toward the pressure axis means lower compliance.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient's flow-volume loop shows a scooped, reduced expiratory limb. What does this loop primarily assess?
questions.explanation: Flow-volume loops primarily assess resistance; a scooped expiratory limb suggests obstruction.

questions.stem: Which conditions DECREASE compliance on a P–V loop? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Decreased compliance means more pressure for the same volume: PE, bronchoconstriction, PTX, insufflation, inadequate relaxation.

questions.stem: A patient with severe emphysema has a P-V loop that rotates toward the volume axis. What change does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue, increasing compliance so more volume enters for the same pressure.

questions.stem: After insufflation, the same 500 mL tidal volume now requires 32 cmH2O instead of 20. How does the P-V loop change?
options: It flattens toward the pressure axis
It rotates toward the volume axis
It opens into a wide hysteresis
questions.explanation: Lower compliance means more pressure for the same volume, flattening the loop toward the pressure axis.

questions.stem: A partially kinked ETT increases airway resistance. How does the flow-volume loop change?
questions.explanation: Higher resistance reduces expiratory flow, flattening the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop.

questions.stem: Which causes increase resistance on a flow–volume loop? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Kinks and bronchospasm raise resistance on the flow-volume loop. Raised abdominal pressure, fibrosis, and obesity reduce compliance instead.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has a high residual volume, prolonged expiration, and a scooped expiratory limb. Which pattern is this?
options: Obstructive: trouble getting air out, with larger volumes
Restrictive: trouble getting air in, with smaller volumes
questions.explanation: Obstructive disease limits expiratory flow and traps air, increasing lung volumes.

questions.stem: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has small lung volumes and a narrow but normally shaped flow-volume loop. Which pattern is this?
options: Restrictive: trouble getting air in, with smaller volumes
Obstructive: trouble getting air out, with larger volumes
questions.explanation: Restrictive disease limits lung expansion, producing smaller volumes with preserved flow shape.

questions.stem: Flow-volume loops show reduced volumes with preserved flow in two patients. Which conditions are restrictive? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Fibrosis and obesity are restrictive. COPD, asthma, bronchospasm, and kinks increase resistance.

questions.stem: During a case, the expiratory limb of the loop starts to flatten before the PIP alarm sounds. Which tool detected the problem early?
questions.explanation: Spirometry loops show changes in compliance and resistance in real time, often before alarms trigger.

questions.stem: After insufflation for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the loops show reduced volumes and higher pressures. Which pattern does this resemble?
options: A leak with a sloped baseline
questions.explanation: Insufflation pushes up the diaphragm and mimics restriction.

questions.stem: The circuit disconnects at the Y-piece during mechanical ventilation. Which alarms should activate? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms are low PIP, low exhaled Vt, and low ETCO2.

questions.stem: Which are the three disconnect alarms? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms are low PIP, low exhaled Vt, and low ETCO2.

questions.stem: How might a small leak be detected before an alarm threshold is reached?
options: Subtle drops in PIP, exhaled volume, or ETCO2
A sudden rise in inspired O2 concentration
A sudden rise in plateau pressure
questions.explanation: Small leaks cause subtle decreases in PIP, exhaled volume, or ETCO2 before alarms trigger.

questions.stem: Besides disconnect alarms, which ventilator alarms help you detect circuit or patient problems? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Other ventilator alarms include high PIP, high PEEP, sustained high pressure, negative pressure, and low O2 supply pressure.

questions.stem: Which ventilator parameters should be scanned during a sweep? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Ventilator parameters include mode, tidal volume and frequency, minute ventilation, peak and mean pressures, PEEP, and loops.

questions.stem: Which gases are displayed as inspired and expired concentrations? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The monitor shows Fi and Et for O2, CO2, air, volatile agent, and N2O.

questions.stem: A patient is moved into steep Trendelenburg and plateau pressure rises from 18 to 26 with unchanged settings. What changed?
questions.explanation: Positioning changes respiratory compliance; a parallel rise in plateau and peak pressure points to compliance.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, Pplat rises from 18 to 28 and PIP from 22 to 32. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A circuit leak at the Y-piece lowering delivered volume
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together, consistent with reduced compliance from insufflation.

questions.stem: During a case, PIP rises from 22 to 40 while Pplat stays 18. Breath sounds are equal, and suctioning returns thick secretions. What was the cause?
questions.explanation: PIP up with stable plateau suggests resistance; secretions fit.

questions.stem: During a laparoscopy, the patient starts coughing against the ventilator, and the P-V loop flattens toward the pressure axis. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Inadequate relaxation increases chest wall stiffness and decreases compliance.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS is ventilated with plateau pressures near 30. Why monitor spirometry loops continuously?
options: To estimate cardiac output from pressure changes
questions.explanation: Real-time loops help detect overdistension or derecruitment and guide settings to prevent lung injury.

questions.stem: Your machine's O2 analyzer responds within seconds and needs no consumable sensor. It works because oxygen is attracted to a magnetic field. Which type is it?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers exploit oxygen's attraction to a magnetic field.

questions.stem: Which O2 sensor is consumed during use?
questions.explanation: Galvanic cells generate current from an oxygen-dependent reaction and are consumed.

questions.stem: An older machine's O2 sensor uses a Clark electrode with an applied voltage. Which reaction occurs at the cathode?
questions.explanation: Polarographic (Clark) sensors reduce oxygen at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.

questions.stem: A technician moves the O2 sensor to the expiratory limb to "measure what the patient exhales." Where should it be placed?
questions.explanation: The O2 sensor belongs in the inspired limb to detect hypoxic gas delivery to the patient.

questions.stem: A removable galvanic O2 sensor reads 18% on room air during the morning check. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Galvanic sensors are calibrated to room air (21%) daily and after prolonged use.

questions.stem: You are evaluating a new oxygen analyzer for purchase. Which performance specifications are appropriate?
options: Response in about 2–10 seconds with ±2% accuracy
questions.explanation: Oxygen analyzers target about 2–10 second response time and ±2% accuracy.

questions.stem: Why is inspired O2 monitoring especially important during low-flow anesthesia?
options: Metabolic O2 use can lower circuit FiO2
Low flow increases oxygen toxicity risk
Low flow causes falsely high O2 readings
questions.explanation: With low fresh gas flow, oxygen consumption can reduce the circuit FiO2.

questions.stem: FiO2 reads 0.50 throughout a case, but the patient's SpO2 falls to 84% from a right mainstem intubation. What limitation of inspired O2 monitoring does this show?
options: Adequate FiO2 does not guarantee arterial oxygenation
Inspired O2 monitoring detects intubation errors
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 monitoring confirms delivery, not uptake; patient factors such as endobronchial intubation can still cause hypoxemia.

questions.stem: The circuit disconnects at the Y-piece, and the inspired O2 alarm does not sound. Why?
questions.explanation: The inspired limb still contains fresh gas after a disconnect, so the O2 reading may stay normal.

questions.stem: A galvanic O2 sensor wears out much faster than expected. Which exposure shortens its life?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide exposure shortens galvanic sensor life.

questions.stem: During laser airway surgery on a child, why is FiO2 kept as low as possible?
options: High FiO2 causes retinopathy in all children
questions.explanation: Oxygen enrichment in the airway during laser or cautery use raises fire risk.

questions.stem: A firefighter after smoke inhalation has SpO2 99%, and a patient after benzocaine spray has SpO2 85% despite high FiO2. What explains both readings?
options: COHb falsely raises SpO2; MetHb drives it toward 85%
Anemia and hypovolemia distort the signal
Hypothermia and acidosis shift the curve
Hyperoxia and hypocarbia affect the probe
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb (falsely high) and MetHb (drives readings toward 85%). Co-oximetry is needed.

questions.stem: FiO2 reads 0.6 and seems fine, but the patient has severe ARDS. What does "trust but verify" mean for inspired O2 monitoring?
options: Pair it with blood oxygenation monitoring
Use FiO2 during induction and stop afterward
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 confirms delivery; pair it with SpO2 or ABGs to confirm oxygenation.

questions.stem: A patient asks whether there is any reason not to monitor inspired oxygen during her anesthetic. What is correct?
options: It is contraindicated with nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 monitoring has no clinical contraindications.

questions.stem: Your gas analyzer measures oxygen by detecting pressure changes in the sample line as a magnetic field switches on and off. Which type is it?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers detect pressure changes in switched magnetic fields.

questions.stem: Which O2 sensor measures current as oxygen diffuses through a membrane and is reduced?
questions.explanation: Polarographic sensors measure current as O2 diffuses through a membrane.

questions.stem: What should be verified during daily machine checkout for O2 analyzers?
options: The fresh gas flow meter and the pipeline gauge
questions.explanation: Verify low-O2 alarm limits and calibration during daily checkout.

questions.stem: Your gas analyzer measures CO2, N2O, and volatile agents by how much light each gas absorbs at specific wavelengths. Which technology is this?
questions.explanation: Modern gas analyzers mainly use infrared absorption, measuring how strongly each gas absorbs specific wavelengths.

questions.stem: An infrared capnometer is tuned to a wavelength where CO2 absorbs strongly. Which wavelength is it?
questions.explanation: CO2 absorbs infrared light strongly at about 4.3 microns. The 660 and 940 nm wavelengths are used by pulse oximeters.

questions.stem: What is the typical ETCO2–PaCO2 gradient in a healthy supine patient under GA?
questions.explanation: The gradient is typically around 5 mmHg, from anatomic dead space.

questions.stem: A research protocol uses xenon as an anesthetic. Why will the standard infrared gas analyzer fail to measure it?
options: Xenon does not absorb infrared light
Xenon absorbs at the same wavelength as CO2
Xenon is too soluble to sample
questions.explanation: Infrared analysis requires gases that absorb infrared light; noble gases such as xenon do not.

questions.stem: Immediately after inspiration ends, a normal capnogram remains at zero briefly before the expiratory upstroke begins. Why?
options: Dead space gas is exhaled first
The patient is inhaling fresh gas
questions.explanation: Phase A–B is the exhalation of dead space gas that contains no CO2.

questions.stem: Where on a normal time capnogram is end-tidal CO2 measured?
options: At the end of the alveolar plateau immediately before inspiration
At the start of the expiratory upstroke
At the midpoint of the alveolar plateau
At the end of the inspiratory downstroke
questions.explanation: Point D is the highest CO2 value at end-expiration: the ETCO2.

questions.stem: What occurs during the inspiratory downstroke of a normal capnogram?
options: Fresh gas is inspired and measured CO2 rapidly falls toward baseline
Alveolar gas is sampled at a stable plateau
Dead-space gas is exhaled before CO2 appears
Mixed dead-space and alveolar gas causes the expiratory upstroke
questions.explanation: D–E is the inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas is entrained.

questions.stem: Two patients' capnograms differ: one has a sharp, vertical upstroke, the other a slow, sloped upstroke. What determines the slope of the B–C upstroke?
questions.explanation: The B–C slope reflects the evenness of alveolar emptying; uneven emptying from obstruction slopes the upstroke.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD has a plateau that keeps rising during expiration instead of staying flat. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: An upward-sloping plateau reflects V/Q mismatch, with slow-emptying units releasing higher CO2 late in expiration.

questions.stem: After intubation in an asthmatic, the capnogram shows a slow upstroke and a shark-fin shape, and PIP rises. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A slow upstroke with a shark-fin shape indicates obstruction such as COPD or bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A COPD patient's capnogram shows a progressively rounded transition into the plateau. What does this rounding indicate?
questions.explanation: The more rounded the upstroke and plateau corner, the greater the obstruction.

questions.stem: A normally shaped capnogram with a rising ETCO2 suggests which causes? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A normal shape with rising values means hypoventilation or increased CO2 production.

questions.stem: Which events can cause a transient ETCO2 increase? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Tourniquet release and aortic unclamping wash CO2 from ischemic tissue, transiently raising ETCO2. Hyperventilation lowers it.

questions.stem: The capnogram suddenly goes flat during a stable case. What should you evaluate immediately?
questions.explanation: Sudden waveform loss can mean disconnection, obstruction, arrest, or sampling failure, all of which need immediate evaluation.

questions.stem: What does stable ETCO2 for three breaths confirm about ETT placement?
options: It is not esophageal, but may still be endobronchial
It is correctly placed in the midtrachea
It is not endobronchial and is at the correct depth
It is secure and will not dislodge
questions.explanation: Stable ETCO2 supports non-esophageal placement but does not rule out endobronchial or shallow placement.

questions.stem: During a case, FiO2, ETCO2, and end-tidal sevoflurane all drop sharply at the same moment. What is the MOST likely source?
questions.explanation: When every measured gas changes together, suspect the sampling line or equipment. A single gas changing suggests the patient.

questions.stem: During a case, ETCO2 drops from 38 to 24 while FiO2 and end-tidal sevoflurane are unchanged. Which category is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: A change in one gas points to patient physiology, such as reduced pulmonary perfusion.

questions.stem: Which conditions increase dead space and make ETCO2 underestimate PaCO2? (Select 5)
options: An adult circuit in a small child
questions.explanation: Dead space and V/Q mismatch increase the gradient: PE, emphysema, OLV, low CO.

questions.stem: Why can an adult circuit on a pediatric patient cause falsely low ETCO2?
options: Increased dead space and dilution of exhaled gas
Faster sampling rate from pediatric tubes
Lower resistance in the adult circuit tubing
questions.explanation: Using adult circuits in pediatrics increases dead space and dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A 1.2 kg premature infant is ventilated with a sidestream capnograph. Why might the reading be unreliable?
options: Sampling is a large share of ventilation
questions.explanation: Sidestream sampling of up to about 200 mL/min can be a significant fraction of an infant's ventilation and distort readings.

questions.stem: A 900 g premature infant is ventilated at 6 mL breaths, 40 times per minute, with a sidestream capnograph sampling 150 mL/min. Why is this a problem?
options: The sample is about 60% of minute ventilation
The sample is about 6% of minute ventilation
The sample is too small to matter
Sidestream monitors do not sample gas
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation is 6 × 40 = 240 mL/min; 150 mL/min is about 60% of it, which distorts readings and ventilation.

questions.stem: Condensation keeps occluding a sidestream sampling line during a long humidified case. What simple step reduces water entry?
options: Keep the sampling port pointing up
Lower the sampling line below the circuit
questions.explanation: Positioning the sampling line above the circuit reduces water entering the line.

questions.stem: During a case, the capnogram baseline rises to 6 mmHg between breaths. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A baseline that does not return to zero means the patient is inhaling CO2 (rebreathing).

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 is 6 mmHg during a case. Which causes should you check? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: An elevated inspiratory baseline means rebreathing from exhausted absorbent, faulty valves, low FGF, or miscalibration.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram I. What is the MOST likely cause of the rising baseline on low fresh gas flow?
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent or a sticking valve
A partially kinked ETT with a shark-fin upstroke
questions.explanation: The baseline does not return to zero, indicating rebreathing.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram I. Fresh gas flow is 0.5 L/min, the absorbent has turned purple, and inspired CO2 is 7. What is the BEST immediate action?
options: Raise flow; check absorbent and valves
questions.explanation: Rebreathing from exhausted absorbent and low fresh gas flow is fixed by raising flow and checking absorbent and valves.

questions.stem: A sudden drop in ETCO2 to near zero with loss of waveform can indicate which problems? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Sudden loss suggests malposition, severe hypotension, massive PE, cardiac arrest, or disconnection.

questions.stem: During a laparotomy, the capnogram plateau shows a notch in each breath, and the surgeon says the abdomen is tightening. What does the notch indicate?
questions.explanation: A curare cleft shows spontaneous effort against the ventilator, often from wearing-off NMB.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram H. The notch appears 70 minutes after the last rocuronium dose. What does it MOST suggest?
options: Returning spontaneous effort as blockade wears off
Bronchospasm from surgical stimulation at a light plane
questions.explanation: A notch in the plateau is a curare cleft, showing spontaneous effort.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram H. The surgeon complains of a tight abdomen and the notch persists. What does this suggest, and what should you consider?
questions.explanation: A curare cleft shows the patient is breathing against the ventilator, which may need more paralytic or deeper anesthesia.

questions.stem: During a slow-rate ventilation case, small regular ripples appear on the end of the capnogram, synchronized with the ECG. What are they?
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic oscillations come from heart and great vessel contractions moving gas at end expiration.

questions.stem: The capnogram becomes triangular and sloping, exhaled volume is lower than set, and a hissing sound is heard. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A leak in the circuit or ETT cuff
questions.explanation: A sloping, triangular trace with low exhaled volume suggests a leak in the circuit or cuff.

questions.stem: In a patient on high respiratory rates with stiff lungs, the capnogram curls into a pigtail shape. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A pigtail capnogram suggests poor compliance or breath stacking.

questions.stem: A flat trace with no waveform can mean which problems? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: A flat trace indicates esophageal intubation, disconnection, apnea, or arrest.

questions.stem: Which statement about capnography during TIVA is correct?
options: Expired agent monitoring is irrelevant, but ETCO2 is still required
ETCO2 is not needed during TIVA
Expired agent monitoring is required during TIVA to dose propofol
TIVA requires pulse oximetry in place of capnography
questions.explanation: No gas in means no gas out, but ETCO2 is still required.

questions.stem: Why is expired anesthetic gas monitoring helpful during low-flow anesthesia?
options: It guides volatile titration when circuit concentration differs
It replaces the need for inspired O2 analysis at low flows
It measures depth of anesthesia directly
questions.explanation: Expired agent monitoring helps titrate volatile agents, especially with low flows.

questions.stem: Capnography is required during which situations? (Select 2)
options: Recovery on a postoperative surgical floor
questions.explanation: Capnography is standard during GA and required during moderate and deep sedation.

questions.stem: What does a sudden drop in ETCO2 with a preserved waveform MOST suggest?
options: Reduced pulmonary blood flow, such as embolism
Esophageal intubation with washout of swallowed CO2
questions.explanation: A sudden fall with waveform present suggests reduced perfusion.

questions.stem: A patient has ETCO2 of 28 with an ABG PaCO2 of 50. What does this gradient suggest?
options: Increased dead space or V/Q mismatch
Normal gradient for a healthy patient
questions.explanation: A 22 mmHg gradient indicates increased dead space or V/Q mismatch.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation, ETCO2 is lower than expected. Why?
options: Dead space and V/Q mismatch increase
questions.explanation: OLV increases dead space and V/Q mismatch, lowering ETCO2 relative to PaCO2.

questions.stem: A neonate with a cuffless ETT has low ETCO2. What is a likely explanation?
options: Leak around the cuffless tube and high sampling rate
Increased CO2 production in neonates relative to adults
questions.explanation: Neonatal cuffless tubes and high sidestream rates can produce falsely low ETCO2.

questions.stem: After CO2 insufflation for a laparoscopy, which capnogram and loop changes are expected?
options: A restrictive pattern with rising ETCO2
An obstructive pattern with falling ETCO2
questions.explanation: Insufflation reduces compliance and CO2 is absorbed from the abdomen, raising ETCO2.

questions.stem: During a hip replacement, ETCO2 falls from 38 to 24 while the waveform shape stays normal and BP drops to 75/40. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A lower ETCO2 with a preserved waveform reflects reduced perfusion, as in hypotension or embolism.

questions.stem: What is the first action when ETCO2 suddenly disappears?
options: Check the patient and airway immediately
Replace the water trap and recalibrate
questions.explanation: Loss of ETCO2 is an emergency until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: ETCO2 rises from 38 to 60 with a normal waveform and stable ventilation. Which cause should be considered?
options: Increased CO2 production, such as MH
Exhausted absorbent with rebreathing of CO2
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with normal shape suggests increased CO2 production or hypoventilation.

questions.stem: In a healthy ventilated patient, which value is the best noninvasive reflection of alveolar CO2?
questions.explanation: ETCO2 approximates alveolar CO2 in patients with normal V/Q matching.

questions.stem: Why does the capnogram baseline normally return to zero during inspiration?
options: The patient inhales fresh gas without CO2
CO2 is absorbed by the lungs during inspiration
The sampling line closes during inspiration
The monitor resets with each breath
questions.explanation: During inspiration, fresh gas containing no CO2 fills the sampling site, returning the baseline to zero.

questions.stem: What does a sudden drop in ETCO2 to near zero with a stable BP suggest?
options: Massive pulmonary embolism with preserved waveform
questions.explanation: Loss of ETCO2 with stable BP often points to disconnection or sampling issues.

questions.stem: During bronchospasm, what does the capnogram show?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm causes a shark-fin shape.

questions.stem: During a long case with heated humidification, the capnogram reading becomes erratic and then disappears. What limitation of capnography explains this?
options: Condensation can occlude the sampling line
Capnography reads falsely low during humidification
questions.explanation: Sampling lines can occlude with condensation, causing erratic or lost readings.

questions.stem: What is the ETCO2 alarm requirement during capnography?
options: It must be audible to the anesthesia team
It may be paused during repositioning
It must be visible but may be silenced
It must be visible on the screen
questions.explanation: The ETCO2 alarm must be audible to the anesthesia provider or team.

questions.stem: The capnogram baseline reads 4 mmHg even before the patient is connected and with fresh gas flowing through the sensor. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: An elevated baseline with no patient connected points to a calibration error.

questions.stem: A patient has a shark-fin capnogram and rising peak pressures. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Shark-fin shape with high pressures suggests obstruction.

questions.stem: During a prone spine case, the capnogram becomes shark-fin shaped and PIP rises to 38. What should you suspect?
questions.explanation: A kinked ETT causes an obstructive shark-fin pattern with high PIP.

questions.stem: ETCO2 rises transiently after releasing a tourniquet. What is the reason?
options: Washout of CO2 from ischemic tissue
Increased dead space from reduced limb perfusion
questions.explanation: Tourniquet release returns CO2 from ischemic tissue.

questions.stem: After intubation, you see three small capnogram waveforms that fade to zero. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Gastric CO2 can produce a few small waveforms that rapidly disappear with esophageal placement.

questions.stem: The low ETCO2 alarm sounds during a case. What is the MOST important response?
questions.explanation: Every capnography alarm requires prompt evaluation of patient, airway, circuit, and perfusion.

questions.stem: During sedation, capnography shows a gradually rising ETCO2 with slower respiratory rate. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with slower RR suggests hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A capnogram shows a sloped plateau and rising ETCO2 in a COPD patient. What is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: COPD causes V/Q mismatch and a sloped plateau.

questions.stem: Which is TRUE about ETCO2 and PaCO2 during pulmonary embolism?
options: ETCO2 falls and the gradient widens
ETCO2 rises and the gradient narrows
questions.explanation: PE increases dead space, lowering ETCO2 and widening the gradient.

questions.stem: You are choosing an ECG lead to detect ischemia during a vascular case. Which lead is MOST sensitive?
questions.explanation: In the Landesberg study, V3 detected ischemia earliest and most often (86.8%), followed by V4 and V5.

questions.stem: In the Landesberg vascular surgery study, what percentage of ischemic events showed ST depression?
questions.explanation: 97% of ischemic events showed ST depression, not elevation.

questions.stem: For a patient with CAD, which pair of leads BEST covers rhythm and ischemia?
questions.explanation: Lead II is best for rhythm; V3 is most sensitive for ischemia.

questions.stem: A patient develops an irregular rhythm with abnormal P waves during a case. Which lead is BEST for evaluating it?
questions.explanation: Lead II aligns with atrial depolarization, so it is best for rhythm and atrial arrhythmia analysis.

questions.stem: A patient's preop 12-lead shows ST depression in V4 and V5. How should you select intraoperative monitoring leads?
options: Choose leads that match his preop changes
Choose leads based on surgical site alone
questions.explanation: Fingerprinting selects leads that match the patient's known preop ECG changes.

questions.stem: A high-risk patient with CAD is monitored with lead II only. What is the risk?
options: Ischemia in other territories may be missed
questions.explanation: A single lead misses ischemia that multiple leads would detect.

questions.stem: You switch from a 3-cable to a 5-cable ECG. How many views does the 5-cable system provide?
questions.explanation: A 5-cable system provides six views; a 3-cable system provides two.

questions.stem: During a chest case, the standard limb leads cannot be placed, so five electrodes are placed in unconventional positions to derive a 12-lead. What system is this?
questions.explanation: EASI derives a 12-lead ECG from unconventional electrode placement.

questions.stem: Which steps are recommended before induction for ECG? (Select 5)
options: Use only one lead for simplicity
questions.explanation: Print a baseline, optimize waveform size, turn ST monitoring on, and verify placement.

questions.stem: A student placed the ECG electrodes, and lead II shows inverted P waves. What is the BEST next step?
options: Treat as an ectopic atrial rhythm
questions.explanation: "Trust but verify" means checking electrode placement even when others applied them.

questions.stem: For a left thoracotomy, the standard left chest electrode position is in the surgical field. What should you do?
options: Move electrodes away from the field
questions.explanation: Surgical site and position may require moving electrodes away from the field.

questions.stem: You want the best ischemia coverage for a patient with prior anterior wall disease. Which leads are preferred? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Preferred ischemia leads are V3 (most sensitive), V4, V5, III, and aVF.

questions.stem: A patient's baseline ECG shows changes in III and aVF. Which leads should be prioritized?
questions.explanation: Fingerprinting prioritizes leads with baseline changes.

questions.stem: During transport from the OR table to the stretcher, the ECG is disconnected for 5 minutes before leaving the room. What does ASA require?
options: Continuous display until leaving the room
questions.explanation: ASA requires continuous ECG display from the start of anesthesia until leaving the room.

questions.stem: In the Landesberg study, V3 detected ischemia most often. Which lead was second most sensitive?
questions.explanation: Landesberg found V3 most sensitive (86.8%), then V4 (78.9%), then V5 (65.8%).

questions.stem: Which ECG change is MOST likely during perioperative ischemia?
questions.explanation: Most ischemic events show ST depression.

questions.stem: What bladder size is correct for an NIBP cuff?
options: Width about 40% and length about 80% of arm circumference
Width about 20% and length about 50% of arm circumference
Width about 60% and length about 100% of arm circumference
Width about 80% and length about 40% of arm circumference
questions.explanation: A correct cuff has a bladder width of 40% and length of 80% of arm circumference.

questions.stem: A patient with a 40 cm arm circumference is measured with a standard adult cuff. The BP reads 168/96, but her arterial line reads 132/78. What explains this?
options: A cuff that is too small reads falsely high
A cuff that is too large reads falsely high
questions.explanation: An undersized cuff needs higher pressure to occlude the artery, falsely raising the reading.

questions.stem: A thin patient is measured with a thigh cuff on her arm, and the BP reads 92/50. A correctly sized cuff reads 118/72. What explains this?
options: A cuff that is too large reads falsely low
A cuff that is too small reads falsely low
The arm is above heart level
questions.explanation: An oversized cuff occludes the artery at lower pressure, falsely lowering the reading.

questions.stem: If the cuffed limb is below heart level, what happens to the reading?
questions.explanation: A limb below the heart gives falsely high readings.

questions.stem: If the cuffed limb is above heart level, what happens to the reading?
questions.explanation: A limb above the heart gives falsely low readings.

questions.stem: Forearm BP measurements tend to do what?
questions.explanation: Forearm measurements can overestimate BP.

questions.stem: An NIBP cuff cycles every minute on the same arm during a 6-hour case. Which complications can result? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Repeated cuff cycling can cause nerve injury, compartment syndrome, and IV interference.

questions.stem: Where should NIBP be placed if an IV is in one arm?
options: On the same arm as the IV
On the forearm of the IV arm
questions.explanation: Use the contralateral limb to avoid IV interference.

questions.stem: NIBP should be avoided over which sites? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Avoid repeated cuff occlusion over fractures, open injuries, fistulas, or PICC lines.

questions.stem: Why is caution needed after axillary lymph node dissection?
options: Risk of edema, skin injury, and nerve compression
Risk of falsely low readings without tissue injury
questions.explanation: Repeated cuff inflation can worsen edema and cause injury.

questions.stem: An oscillometric NIBP measures pulsations in the cuff during deflation. At which point does the device identify MAP?
options: At the point of maximal oscillation amplitude
At the midpoint between first and last oscillation
questions.explanation: MAP corresponds to maximal oscillation amplitude; systolic and diastolic are derived by algorithm.

questions.stem: A patient's BP is 150/90. What is the approximate MAP?
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 90 + 60/3 = 110 mmHg.

questions.stem: During a code, the NIBP fails, so you inflate the cuff and feel for the radial pulse as it deflates. The pulse returns at 85 mmHg. What does this value estimate?
questions.explanation: Palpation estimates systolic pressure as the pulse returns during deflation.

questions.stem: During manual BP measurement, sounds appear at 140 mmHg and disappear at 85 mmHg. What do these points estimate?
questions.explanation: Korotkoff sounds estimate systolic pressure when they appear and diastolic when they disappear.

questions.stem: When does NIBP predictive usefulness decline during changing hemodynamics?
options: It holds steady if the cuff is correctly sized
questions.explanation: The chapter suggests usefulness declines when intervals exceed about 3 minutes.

questions.stem: In a premature infant with a PDA, which arm best reflects cerebral perfusion?
questions.explanation: The right arm is preductal, reflecting blood that perfuses the brain.

questions.stem: Which factors impair NIBP reliability? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Low flow, stiffness, motion, arrhythmia, leaks, and rapid deflation impair reliability.

questions.stem: You are about to induce a 70-year-old with hypertension. How should you set the NIBP cycle?
options: Every 10 minutes to reduce cuff trauma
questions.explanation: More frequent BP measurement is recommended during induction because induction agents cause rapid changes.

questions.stem: What is the minimum NIBP frequency during anesthesia?
questions.explanation: BP must be recorded at least every 5 minutes.

questions.stem: Why might more frequent BP checks be needed in patients with IHD?
options: Higher risk of perioperative MI and instability
IHD requires invasive monitoring in every case
questions.explanation: Limited reserve and IHD warrant closer monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient with a BMI of 52 has a conical upper arm. Why is cuff selection critical?
options: Larger, conical arms affect fit and accuracy
Obese patients need a smaller cuff for a tight fit
Arterial lines are contraindicated in obesity
questions.explanation: Arm size and shape change cuff fit, so an appropriately sized cuff or alternative site is needed.

questions.stem: A patient has bilateral arm fistulas and both arms are tucked. Where can NIBP be measured?
options: On the forearm over an IV
Nowhere, so BP is not measured
questions.explanation: The lower extremity is an alternative when the upper arms are unavailable.

questions.stem: A patient's NIBP is 180/100 with a cuff that is too small. What is the MOST likely true BP?
questions.explanation: A small cuff overestimates BP.

questions.stem: A patient's arm is elevated above heart level during surgery. NIBP reads 90/50. What is MOST likely?
options: The true BP may be higher than displayed
The true BP is lower than displayed
The reading is accurate because the cuff is sized correctly
questions.explanation: Limb above heart level produces falsely low readings.

questions.stem: Which statement about oscillometric NIBP is correct?
options: Systolic and diastolic are estimated with device algorithms
Systolic is measured directly from Korotkoff sounds by the device
MAP is calculated from pulse pressure
questions.explanation: SBP and DBP are estimated using device-specific algorithms.

questions.stem: For a carotid endarterectomy in a patient with prior TIA, which additional monitors might you add beyond standard ASA monitors? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Additional monitors include cerebral oximetry, BIS, invasive pressure, precordial stethoscope, TEE, and ICP monitoring as indicated.

questions.stem: During cross-clamping for a carotid endarterectomy, you want to detect falling cerebral oxygen delivery. Which monitor is designed for this?
questions.explanation: Cerebral oximetry is used in carotid surgery to detect reduced cerebral oxygenation.

questions.stem: During a sitting craniotomy, you place a precordial stethoscope. What sound are you listening for?
options: A mill-wheel murmur from venous air embolism
questions.explanation: A precordial stethoscope can detect the mill-wheel murmur of air embolism, a form of PE.

questions.stem: You plan to use processed EEG to guide depth. When should you obtain a baseline reading?
questions.explanation: A BIS baseline should be obtained before induction to interpret later values.

questions.stem: For a calm 8-year-old having a mask induction, when should monitors ideally be applied?
options: While the child is awake, if tolerated
After induction, to avoid upsetting the child
Pulse oximetry alone until the IV is placed
questions.explanation: Starting monitors while the child is awake provides baseline values, when the child tolerates it.

questions.stem: A patient is in beach chair position with the arterial transducer taped to the bed rail at hip level. Where should it be zeroed and leveled?
options: At the level of the arterial catheter
questions.explanation: Transducers are zeroed and leveled at the right atrium; errors in height change the displayed pressure.

questions.stem: Before treating an abrupt arterial pressure change, what should you verify first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Verify leveling, tubing, catheter patency, and waveform fidelity before treating.

questions.stem: You are placing an arterial line for a routine major case. Which artery is MOST commonly cannulated?
questions.explanation: The radial artery is the most common site for arterial cannulation.

questions.stem: Before placing a radial arterial line, a colleague performs the Allen test and reports it is normal. How reliable is this?
options: It is required before every radial line
questions.explanation: The Allen test has not been confirmed as a reliable predictor of ischemic complications.

questions.stem: A hypotensive patient with weak, thready radial pulses needs an arterial line. When does ultrasound help most?
options: When pulses are weak or vessels are small
questions.explanation: Ultrasound improves success when pulses are weak or vessels small.

questions.stem: Which are indications for an arterial line? (Select 2)
options: Anticipated rapid or extreme BP changes
Routine knee arthroscopy in an ASA II patient
Short outpatient procedure with no risk
questions.explanation: Arterial lines are indicated for expected rapid BP changes and vasoactive titration, as well as frequent labs and respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Which are contraindications to arterial cannulation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Compromised collateral flow, local infection, or proximal injury/thrombosis prevent accurate readings.

questions.stem: An arterial line reads 168/60, while the NIBP reads 140/64 and MAPs agree. The fast-flush shows multiple oscillations. What is happening?
options: The NIBP cuff is too small
questions.explanation: Underdamping causes systolic overshoot of about 15–30 mmHg, while MAP remains accurate.

questions.stem: An arterial line trace looks rounded with no dicrotic notch, and its systolic is 20 mmHg lower than the NIBP. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: Overdamping from air, clot, or kinks blunts the trace and underestimates systolic.

questions.stem: Which factors degrade arterial line fidelity? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Air bubbles, long tubing, stopcocks, clots, and kinks degrade fidelity.

questions.stem: Refer to the fast-flush test. Which trace shows optimal damping?
options: Trace 1, with one or two oscillations
questions.explanation: Optimal damping shows one or two oscillations before returning to baseline.

questions.stem: Refer to the fast-flush test. Trace 2 shows many oscillations after the flush. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Multiple oscillations after a fast flush indicate an underdamped system.

questions.stem: Refer to the fast-flush test. Trace 3 returns slowly to baseline with no oscillations. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A slow return without oscillations indicates overdamping, often from air or clot.

questions.stem: A patient's arterial line shows many oscillations after a fast flush. What is the MOST likely effect on SBP?
questions.explanation: Underdamped systems overestimate SBP.

questions.stem: A patient's arterial line shows no oscillations and a sluggish return after fast flush. What is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Overdamping often comes from air bubbles or clot.

questions.stem: You squeeze the flush device and watch the trace oscillate. What does this fast-flush test estimate?
questions.explanation: The fast-flush test estimates damping coefficient and natural frequency of the system.

questions.stem: An arterial line's readings are inaccurate despite correct leveling. Which properties determine its dynamic fidelity?
questions.explanation: Dynamic fidelity depends on damping and natural frequency.

questions.stem: On an arterial waveform, a small notch appears on the downslope after the systolic peak. What does this represent?
questions.explanation: The dicrotic notch marks aortic valve closure.

questions.stem: On the arterial waveform, what is the lowest point before the next upstroke?
questions.explanation: The lowest point is the DBP.

questions.stem: The arterial monitor shows a MAP that differs from the formula estimate. How does the monitor derive MAP?
options: From the area under the arterial curve
questions.explanation: The monitor calculates MAP as the average pressure from the area under the curve.

questions.stem: A patient's arterial BP is 160/60. What is the pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 160 − 60 = 100 mmHg.

questions.stem: A patient has a radial and a dorsalis pedis arterial line. The pedal systolic is 20 mmHg higher than radial, though MAPs match. Why?
options: The pedal transducer is too high
questions.explanation: Systolic pressure rises as the pulse travels peripherally because of wave reflection; MAP stays similar.

questions.stem: In patients with severe PVD, which BP value should be used?
questions.explanation: Use the greater value in severe PVD.

questions.stem: While flushing an arterial line, a nurse squeezes the flush device with air in the tubing. What complication can result?
questions.explanation: Pressurized flush systems can push air into the artery, causing embolism.

questions.stem: A neonate's arterial line flush runs for 24 hours at the standard continuous rate. About how much fluid does this add?
questions.explanation: At 3–6 mL/hr, a continuous flush adds about 72–144 mL per day, which is significant for a neonate.

questions.stem: A patient has had a radial arterial line for 3 days in the ICU. Which complications should you watch for? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Arterial line complications include hematoma, thrombosis, ischemia, embolism, infection, nerve injury, hemorrhage, and air embolism.

questions.stem: Which pediatric arterial sites are common? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Common pediatric sites include umbilical, radial, and femoral.

questions.stem: A neonate has an umbilical artery catheter. Which complications are associated with it?
questions.explanation: Umbilical artery catheters carry risks of aortic thrombosis and coarctation.

questions.stem: An arterial line connects through 2 m of tubing and four stopcocks. The trace is distorted. Which change improves accuracy?
questions.explanation: Minimal tubing length and few stopcocks improve arterial line fidelity.

questions.stem: A transducer is accidentally lowered 10 cm below the right atrium. What happens to BP readings?
questions.explanation: A transducer below RA level reads falsely high due to hydrostatic pressure.

questions.stem: A transducer is raised above the right atrium. What happens to BP readings?
questions.explanation: Raising the transducer above RA level lowers readings.

questions.stem: Why can radial artery pressure underestimate central pressure in some cases?
options: Increased wave reflection in the radial artery
questions.explanation: Hand vascular resistance changes can make radial pressures underestimate central pressures.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter compares absorption at two wavelengths to calculate SpO2. Which wavelengths are used?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximeters use 660 nm (red) and 940 nm (infrared) light.

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry calculates saturation from how much light passes through tissue. Which law underlies this?
questions.explanation: The Beer-Lambert law relates light absorption to concentration and path length.

questions.stem: How does a pulse oximeter separate arterial blood from venous blood and tissue?
options: It uses a third wavelength for tissue
questions.explanation: Plethysmography separates the pulsatile arterial component from nonpulsatile tissue and venous signal.

questions.stem: What type of saturation does SpO2 measure?
questions.explanation: SpO2 is functional saturation; co-oximetry measures fractional.

questions.stem: Methemoglobinemia tends to drive SpO2 toward what value?
questions.explanation: MetHb absorbs red and IR 1:1, driving SpO2 toward ~85%.

questions.stem: How does carboxyhemoglobin affect SpO2?
options: No predictable effect on the displayed saturation
questions.explanation: COHb causes falsely high SpO2.

questions.stem: Which conditions shift the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Hypercapnia, acidosis, and hyperthermia shift the curve right. Fetal hemoglobin, alkalosis, and hypothermia shift it left.

questions.stem: A septic patient is febrile and acidotic. How does this shift the oxyhemoglobin curve, and what is the effect?
options: Right shift; better tissue O2 release
questions.explanation: Fever and acidosis shift the curve right, decreasing affinity and releasing oxygen to tissues.

questions.stem: An ABG shows PaO2 60 mmHg in a patient breathing room air in PACU. What SpO2 would you expect?
questions.explanation: PaO2 60 corresponds to about 90% saturation, near the steep part of the curve.

questions.stem: What happens once PaO2 falls onto the steep portion of the curve?
options: PaO2 rises in step with SpO2 on this portion
questions.explanation: Desaturation accelerates on the steep portion.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter reads 92%. Within what range is the true saturation likely to fall?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry accuracy is about ±2–3% between 70% and 100%.

questions.stem: Which factors impair pulse oximetry accuracy? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Motion, low perfusion, hypothermia, dyes, nail polish, ambient light, and cautery impair accuracy.

questions.stem: A sedated patient on 6 L nasal cannula becomes apneic. SpO2 stays 99% for 4 minutes. Why is pulse oximetry a poor indicator of ventilation?
options: Supplemental O2 delays desaturation after apnea
questions.explanation: With supplemental oxygen, patients can be apneic for minutes before SpO2 falls.

questions.stem: In pediatric anesthesia, pulse oximetry is more sensitive than capnography for detecting what?
options: Esophageal intubation before CO2 fades from the trace
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is more sensitive than capnography for mainstem intubation in pediatrics.

questions.stem: A patient in septic shock has SpO2 of 98%, but lactate is rising and she is mottled. What does pulse oximetry NOT measure?
questions.explanation: SpO2 measures arterial saturation, not oxygen delivery to or use by tissues.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has SpO2 99% but is confused. Which device can identify COHb?
questions.explanation: Co-oximeters use multiple wavelengths to distinguish COHb and MetHb.

questions.stem: A patient with CO poisoning has SpO2 99%. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: SpO2 is falsely high; co-oximetry is needed
The probe is misplaced on a vasoconstricted finger
questions.explanation: COHb causes falsely high SpO2.

questions.stem: A patient receives methylene blue and SpO2 drops. Why?
questions.explanation: Dyes impair oximeter accuracy.

questions.stem: A patient asks if there is any reason not to use a pulse oximeter on her. What is correct?
options: It is contraindicated in sickle cell
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry has no clinical contraindications.

questions.stem: During deep hypothermic arrest at 18 °C, the pulse oximeter loses its signal. Why?
options: Poor perfusion reduces the pulsatile signal
questions.explanation: Extreme hypothermia causes vasoconstriction and poor perfusion, reducing the pulsatile signal.

questions.stem: A patient in a cold OR is losing heat. Which mechanism accounts for the largest share?
questions.explanation: Radiation is the largest source of heat loss under anesthesia.

questions.stem: During an open abdominal case, 200 g of water evaporates from the exposed bowel. About how much heat is lost?
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes about 0.58 kcal per gram of water: 200 × 0.58 = 116 kcal.

questions.stem: Which are core temperature sites? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Core sites include bladder, distal esophagus, ear canal, trachea, nasopharynx, rectum, and pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: A patient's core temperature is 36 °C and skin temperature is 32 °C. What is the approximate mean body temperature?
Which site may lag during active cooling or rewarming?
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature can lag during rapid changes.

questions.stem: A patient's skin temperature reads 33 °C but his esophageal temperature is 36.5 °C. Which value represents body heat content?
options: Neither alone; skin poorly reflects mean temperature
Skin, since it reflects heat loss
Esophageal alone, since it equals mean body temperature
An average of the two with equal weighting
questions.explanation: Skin temperature does not adequately represent mean body temperature, which weights core 0.85 and skin 0.15.

questions.stem: During a sevoflurane case, ETCO2 rises from 38 to 70 despite increased ventilation, and HR climbs to 130. Temperature is 37.2 °C. A colleague says it cannot be MH since there's no fever. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Hyperthermia is a late sign of MH
MH begins with fever in most cases
questions.explanation: Hypercarbia and tachycardia are early MH signs; hyperthermia appears late.

questions.stem: At the end of a 6-hour case, a patient's temperature is 34.9 °C. Which complications should you expect? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Hypothermia raises oxygen consumption, impairs coagulation, slows drug metabolism, and increases infection and ischemia risk.

questions.stem: A patient is lightly sedated for a 30-minute hand case under a block. Is continuous temperature monitoring useful?
options: Often not, since thermoregulation is intact
Yes, it is required for all sedation
Yes, skin temperature is the best guide
questions.explanation: Continuous temperature monitoring is often uninformative in conscious patients with intact thermoregulation.

questions.stem: During a cardiac case with a PA catheter, which temperature site gives the strongest estimate of core temperature?
questions.explanation: PA blood temperature is a strong core temperature estimate.

questions.stem: A patient under a spinal and another under GA both become hypothermic. How do these anesthetics affect thermoregulation?
options: Both inhibit afferent and efferent control
GA inhibits thermoregulation; neuraxial spares it
GA affects thermoregulation but neuraxial does not
questions.explanation: Both general and regional anesthesia impair afferent and efferent thermoregulatory control.

questions.stem: A patient in a cold OR loses heat to the walls, the cold table, and moving air. Which mechanisms are involved? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Heat is lost by radiation (the largest), conduction, convection, and evaporation.

questions.stem: A patient is actively rewarmed after cardiopulmonary bypass. Why might multiple temperature sites be needed?
options: Different sites change at different rates
Rectal temperature is the accurate reference
Skin temperature is the best guide
PA temperature lags behind rectal during rewarming
questions.explanation: During cooling or rewarming, sites change at different rates.

questions.stem: A 20-minute cataract case and a 6-hour open case are scheduled. When does ASA require temperature monitoring?
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring is required when significant temperature changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected.

questions.stem: After intubation, ETCO2 reads 34, 22, 9, then 0 over four breaths while SpO2 is 98%. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Esophageal intubation with washout of swallowed CO2
Bronchospasm causing a shark-fin trace that flattens
Right mainstem intubation reducing ventilated lung
Sampling line occlusion from condensation in the trap
questions.explanation: CO2 that fades over a few breaths after intubation is esophageal until proven otherwise; SpO2 lags.

questions.stem: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy: PIP goes from 22 to 34 and Pplat from 18 to 30 right after insufflation. ETCO2 rises slowly from 36 to 44. What BEST explains both findings?
options: Reduced compliance plus CO2 absorption from pneumoperitoneum
Bronchospasm with rising airway resistance and hypoventilation
A kinked ETT with rebreathing through the expiratory valve
Malignant hyperthermia with rising CO2 production and rigidity
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together (compliance), and ETCO2 rose gradually from CO2 absorption.

questions.stem: During a case, low exhaled Vt, low PIP, and low ETCO2 alarms all sound together. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: Pulmonary embolism with increased dead space
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms firing together point to disconnection.

questions.stem: A small cuff leak develops. Which early signs may appear before alarms? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A small leak causes subtle drops in PIP, exhaled volume, and ETCO2 before thresholds.

questions.stem: Mid-case, ETCO2 creeps up and the inspired CO2 reads 7 mmHg. FGF is 0.5 L/min. What is the BEST first move?
options: Raise fresh gas flow and check the absorbent and valves
Increase tidal volume and respiratory rate
Deepen anesthesia to lower CO2 production
Give albuterol for presumed bronchospasm and recheck
questions.explanation: Inspired CO2 means rebreathing; higher FGF compensates while you check absorbent and valves.

questions.stem: A COPD patient's capnogram shows a slanted upstroke and ETCO2 of 45. ABG PaCO2 is 58. What explains the gradient?
options: V/Q mismatch and dead space from obstructive disease
Rebreathing from exhausted absorbent in the circuit
